top_evidence.section: Risk Of Bias In Individual Studies
top_evidence.text: Risk of bias (quality) of individual studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [19]. The MMAT assessed included studies based on the study design; qualitative only, quantitative (non-randomised, randomised, descriptive), or mixed methods. Risk of bias was assessed by two independent researchers, with any discrepancies resolved through discussion or a third reviewer. Studies were not allocated a rating based on recommendations from the MMAT author [19].

top_evidence.text: The database searches resulted in the identification of 12,459 records (Fig. 1). After removing duplicates, 6,129 unique records were retained for screening (Fig. 1). Title and abstract screening resulted in 98 records for further screening. Of these, 11 reports could not be retrieved (abstract-only, n = 7; non-written format, n = 2; inaccessible, n = 2), leaving 87 articles retained for full-text screening (Fig. 1). Thirteen articles were eligible for inclusion following the final screening stage (Fig. 1). This reduction highlights the limited availability of recent evidence investigating POC testing and health literacy outcomes.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity in intervention type (e.g. community screening vs. clinical monitoring), disease focus (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular), outcome measurement tools (e.g. Patient Activation Measure, PAM-13; behaviour change), and population characteristics, which restricted comparability. We therefore employed a framework-guided narrative synthesis. Qualitative and quantitative outcome data were extracted and deductively coded against the five WHO health literacy actions ( Access , Understand , Appraise , Remember , Use ) to enable thematic comparison. Each outcome was mapped to the domains that best reflected the construct measured, and findings were then categorised by condition and type of POC test.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Background Health literacy responsiveness has been identified as a key action area in reducing the burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), which are a leading cause of death worldwide. Point-of-care (POC) testing has the potential to improve health literacy in individuals and communities. This systematic review aimed to synthesise the literature regarding POC testing for NCDs and health literacy outcomes. Methods A systematic search was conducted across seven databases, Medline (via OVID), PsycINFO, Emcare, Scopus, ProQuest (Health databases), CINAHL, and Web of Science, between May 2018 and May 2023. Studies that investigated the utilisation of a POC device for measurement of NCD markers, and reported at least one outcome measure of health literacy in individuals over 10 years old were eligible for inclusion. Risk of bias in included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Results were mapped to the five WHO health literacy actions through narrative synthesis. Results Thirteen studies were eligible for inclusion, primarily investigating POC assessment of diabetes, with some examining lipids or coagulation. Study cohorts were geographically limited to eight countries in predominantly high-income settings. Following POC testing relevant to diabetes and cardiovascular contexts, patients reported an enhanced understanding of health, motivation to make positive lifestyle changes, increased quality of life and decreased worry, increased confidence, and improved health markers. Conclusion The findings from this review suggest that POC testing may support improvements in individual health literacy outcomes relevant to NCD management, specifically in diabetes and cardiovascular contexts. These findings reflect the potential of POC testing to contribute to more responsive health systems, by improving accessibility, results delivery, and communication of health information. However, the evidence base is limited in scope, and findings may not necessarily be generalisable. Future studies should prioritise examining a broader range of NCDs, particularly in underdeveloped regions, and employ specific validated health literacy tools. Prospero registration CRD42022348011. top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Thirteen studies were included in the review, with a total sample size of 21,265. Studies assessed POC testing exposures for management of diabetes [20-30], lipids [20, 30] and/or coagulation [29, 31, 32] (Table 1). Although chronic respiratory diseases were included in the search scope, no eligible studies assessing health literacy outcomes were identified. Across conditions, POC testing was implemented in varying contexts, including adult outpatient care [23, 24], paediatric diabetes management (with parental health literacy outcomes) [21, 22], at-home self-testing (e.g. INR testing) [31, 32], and communitybased screening [27, 30]. Health literacy outcomes were reported through a range of proxy measures, including patient activation [25, 28], patient knowledge and experiences [21, 31, 32], Likert scale ratings of understanding [29, 30], qualitative interviews [20-24, 27], medication adherence [26, 31, 32], and behaviour change [21, 30]. As detailed in Table 2, measurement tools varied widely, including validated instruments such as PAM-13, clinical indicators (i.e. HbA1c, INR, and PDC), and study-developed questionnaires, knowledge scores, Likert scales, and qualitative interviews. Included studies were conducted in eight countries: England, India, Ireland, Italy, New Zealand, South Korea, and the United States. The mean ages of adults assessed ranged from 31 to 70 years, with two studies assessing parental outcomes of children with type 1 diabetes [21, 22]. Basic demographic characteristics such as age and sex were consistently reported, however reporting of ethnicity was varied, with most studies not reporting data. Where reported, participants were predominantly European or non-Hispanic White [21-23, 28, 30], with limited representation of minority groups such as Asian or African ethnicity groups [23, 30]. One study included only Black men [27]. Other equity considerations, particularly socioeconomic status, were rarely reported, limiting synthesis across population subgroups. A summary of the included studies can be seen in Table 1.
